Comparing Models for Eyewitness Identification Data

Colin G. Tredoux

Tamsyn M. Naylor

2026-10-29

Source: vignettes/model_comparison.Rmd
model_comparison.Rmd

Acknowledgement. Large language models supplied by Anthropic and OpenAI were used in preparing this vignette, to assist with checking code, testing the veracity of the approaches described, and on occasion editing the text. Responsibility for the content rests with the authors.

Introduction

Eyewitness identification data can be analyzed using multiple theoretical frameworks, each providing unique insights. This vignette demonstrates how to use r4lineups’ model comparison framework to fit and compare:

  1. 2-HT Model (Winter et al., 2022): Multinomial Processing Tree model
  2. EIG (Starns et al., 2023): Expected Information Gain
  3. Full ROC (Smith & Yang, 2020): Receiver Operating Characteristic

The compare_models() function provides a unified interface for fitting all models and generating comparison tables and visualizations.

The Three Models

2-HT Model: Latent Cognitive Processes

The Two-High Threshold (2-HT) model is a multinomial processing tree (MPT) that separates identification decisions into distinct latent processes:

Parameters: - dP: Detection of culprit presence (0-1) - dA: Detection of culprit absence (0-1) - b: Biased suspect selection (0-1) - g: Guessing-based selection (0-1)

Model equations (target-present): - P(suspect ID) = dP + (1-dP) × [b + (1-b) × g × (1/L)] - P(filler ID) = (1-dP) × (1-b) × g × ((L-1)/L) - P(reject) = (1-dP) × (1-b) × (1-g)

Use when: - You want to understand underlying cognitive mechanisms - Testing theories about detection vs. guessing - Comparing conditions with different bias levels

EIG: Information-Theoretic Measure

Expected Information Gain quantifies how much information witness responses provide about guilt vs. innocence using Shannon entropy:

Formula: EIG = Σ p(x) × [H(prior) - H(p(guilty|x))]

where x = response category (e.g., “suspect_high_confidence”)

Interpretation: - EIG = 0: No information (responses don’t distinguish guilty/innocent) - EIG = 1: Perfect information (complete resolution of uncertainty) - Higher EIG = more diagnostic procedure

Use when: - Evaluating overall diagnosticity of procedures - Comparing different identification methods - Assessing policy-relevant cutoffs

Full ROC: Investigator Discriminability

Full ROC uses ALL witness responses (suspect IDs, filler IDs, rejections) to compute a threshold-free measure of discriminability:

Measure: - AUC (Area Under the Curve) - Range: 0.5 (chance) to 1.0 (perfect)

Use when: - Measuring investigator discriminability - Comparing system variables (lineup procedures) - Need threshold-free performance measure

Basic Model Comparison

Loading Data 

library(r4lineups)

lineup_data <- as.data.frame(simulate_lineup_data(
  n_tp        = 300,
  n_ta        = 300,
  d_prime     = 1.5,
  c_criterion = 0.9,   # see the note below: 0 would be far too liberal
  lineup_size = 6,
  conf_levels = 5,
  foil_bias   = c(0.4, 0.2, 0.0, -0.4, -1.0),
  seed        = 2024
))

head(lineup_data)
#>   participant_id target_present lineup_member suspect_pos identification
#> 1             64           TRUE             1           1        suspect
#> 2             89           TRUE             1           1        suspect
#> 3            573          FALSE             2           1         filler
#> 4            393          FALSE             0           1         reject
#> 5            188           TRUE             3           1         filler
#> 6            526          FALSE             3           1         filler
#>   confidence
#> 1          5
#> 2          3
#> 3          5
#> 4          1
#> 5          2
#> 6          5

The c_criterion = 0.9 is not incidental, and it is worth explaining because getting it wrong makes one of the three models impossible to fit.

c_criterion is a threshold on the maximum of the lineup members’ memory strengths, not a textbook signal-detection criterion. The maximum of six draws from a standard normal averages about 1.27, so a criterion of 0 — the function default — is cleared by almost every lineup, and produces a rejection rate near zero:

too_liberal <- as.data.frame(simulate_lineup_data(
  n_tp = 300, n_ta = 300, d_prime = 1.5, c_criterion = 0,
  lineup_size = 6, conf_levels = 5, seed = 2024
))

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    `c_criterion` = c(0, 0.9),
    `Rejection rate (%)` = round(100 * c(
      mean(too_liberal$identification == "reject"),
      mean(lineup_data$identification == "reject")
    ), 1),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Rejection rate under two decision criteria, simulated data (300 target-present and 300 target-absent lineups)."
)
Rejection rate under two decision criteria, simulated data (300 target-present and 300 target-absent lineups).
c_criterion Rejection rate (%)
0.0 0.2
0.9 20.5

The 2-HT model’s detect-absence parameter dA is identified almost entirely by rejections — it is the probability of correctly concluding the culprit is absent. With half a percent of witnesses rejecting, the likelihood is nearly flat in dA and the fit fails. fit_winter_2ht() now detects this and says so; earlier versions failed with an opaque message about non-finite differences, and compare_models() simply omitted the model from its results, so every downstream section that referred to it silently produced nothing.

Comparing All Models 

# Fit all three models
comparison <- compare_models(
  lineup_data,
  models = c("2ht", "eig", "fullroc"),
  lineup_size = 6,
  prior_guilt = 0.5
)

# View comparison table
print(comparison)

Method-Choice Guidance

These methods estimate different quantities; their displayed numbers are not a common model-selection scale and the wrapper does not declare a “best model.”

When to Use Each Model

Use 2-HT when: - Testing cognitive theories (detection, guessing, bias) - Need to separate memory from response bias - Comparing procedures that might differ in bias - Want to understand latent psychological processes

Use EIG when: - Evaluating overall diagnosticity - Comparing identification procedures - Need a single summary measure - Want information-theoretic interpretation

Use Full ROC when: - Need threshold-free discriminability measure - Comparing system variables - Want to use all available information - Policy/practical decision-making focus

Comparing Model Fits

The 2-HT fit reports AIC/BIC, but these values are comparative rather than absolute. They can only be compared with alternative likelihood models fitted to the same observations and outcome representation; they cannot be compared with EIG or AUC. A single-condition 2-HT fit is saturated.

cat("2-HT Model Fit:\n")
#> 2-HT Model Fit:
cat("  AIC:", round(comparison$fitted_models$`2ht`$aic, 2), "\n")
#>   AIC: 1123.62
cat("  BIC:", round(comparison$fitted_models$`2ht`$bic, 2), "\n")
#>   BIC: 1141.21
cat("\nAIC and BIC compare likelihood-based models fitted to the same data.\n")
#> 
#> AIC and BIC compare likelihood-based models fitted to the same data.
cat("EIG and full-ROC AUC are not likelihoods, so they cannot be ranked\n")
#> EIG and full-ROC AUC are not likelihoods, so they cannot be ranked
cat("against the 2-HT model by information criteria.\n")
#> against the 2-HT model by information criteria.

Parameter Recovery Check

A single fit tells you little. The useful check is whether the recovered parameters move as the generating parameter moves:

recovery <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5), function(dp) {
  d <- as.data.frame(simulate_lineup_data(
    n_tp = 400, n_ta = 400, d_prime = dp, c_criterion = 0.9,
    lineup_size = 6, conf_levels = 5,
    foil_bias = c(0.4, 0.2, 0.0, -0.4, -1.0), seed = 500 + round(10 * dp)
  ))
  fit <- fit_winter_2ht(d, lineup_size = 6,
                        target_present = "target_present",
                        identification = "identification")
  data.frame(`True d'` = dp,
             `Recovered dP` = round(fit$parameters[["dP"]], 3),
             `Recovered dA` = round(fit$parameters[["dA"]], 3),
             check.names = FALSE)
}))

knitr::kable(
  recovery, row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "2-HT detection parameters recovered from data simulated at known d', 400 lineups per arm."
)
2-HT detection parameters recovered from data simulated at known d’, 400 lineups per arm.
True d’ Recovered dP Recovered dA
0.5 0.113 0.038
1.0 0.313 0.140
1.5 0.522 0.169
2.0 0.677 0.124
2.5 0.806 0.214

dP increases monotonically with the generating d′, which is the result the check is looking for. It is not on the same scale as d′ and should not be expected to equal it: the two models parameterise memory differently, and what validates the analysis is that the ordering is recovered.

Practical Examples

Example 1: Evaluating a Lineup Procedure

Research question: How well does this lineup procedure discriminate between guilty and innocent suspects?

# Fit all models to assess procedure
procedure_eval <- compare_models(
  lineup_data,
  models = c("2ht", "eig", "fullroc")
)

# Interpretation
cat("Procedure Evaluation:\n\n")
#> Procedure Evaluation:

cat("2-HT: dP =", round(procedure_eval$fitted_models$`2ht`$parameters[["dP"]], 2),
    "\n  → Detection ability is",
    ifelse(procedure_eval$fitted_models$`2ht`$parameters[["dP"]] > 0.5,
           "good", "moderate"), "\n\n")
#> 2-HT: dP = 0.49 
#>   → Detection ability is moderate

if ("eig" %in% procedure_eval$models_fit) {
  cat("EIG =", round(procedure_eval$fitted_models$eig$eig, 3), "bits\n")
  cat("  → Provides",
      round(procedure_eval$fitted_models$eig$eig /
              procedure_eval$fitted_models$eig$prior_entropy * 100, 0),
      "% of maximum information\n\n")
}
#> EIG = 0.187 bits
#>   → Provides 19 % of maximum information

if ("fullroc" %in% procedure_eval$models_fit) {
  cat("Full ROC AUC =", round(procedure_eval$fitted_models$fullroc$auc, 3), "\n")
  cat("  → Discriminability is",
      ifelse(procedure_eval$fitted_models$fullroc$auc > 0.75, "good", "moderate"), "\n")
}
#> Full ROC AUC = 0.747 
#>   → Discriminability is moderate

Example 2: Identifying Sources of Bias

Use 2-HT model to check for bias:

params <- comparison$fitted_models$`2ht`$parameters

bias_param <- params[["b"]]
bias_reading <- if (bias_param < 0.1) {
  "Low: the suspect does not appear to stand out unfairly"
} else if (bias_param > 0.3) {
  "High: the suspect may stand out. Check lineup construction"
} else {
  "Moderate"
}

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(Parameter = "b (biased suspect selection)",
             Estimate = round(bias_param, 3),
             Reading = bias_reading),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "2-HT bias parameter, simulated data (300 target-present and 300 target-absent lineups)."
)
2-HT bias parameter, simulated data (300 target-present and 300 target-absent lineups).
Parameter Estimate Reading
b (biased suspect selection) 0 Low: the suspect does not appear to stand out unfairly

Example 3: Comparing Detection vs. Guessing 

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Parameter = c("dP (detect culprit present)",
                  "dA (detect culprit absent)",
                  "g (guessing-based selection)"),
    Estimate  = round(c(params[["dP"]], params[["dA"]], params[["g"]]), 3)
  ),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "2-HT detection and guessing parameters, simulated data."
)
2-HT detection and guessing parameters, simulated data.
Parameter Estimate
dP (detect culprit present) 0.485
dA (detect culprit absent) 0.049
g (guessing-based selection) 0.754

Detection and guessing are separately identified here, which is the point of the model: an identification rate on its own cannot tell you whether witnesses recognised the culprit or simply picked someone plausible. Note that dP and g are probabilities of different events and are not in competition — a procedure can have both high detection and a high tendency to choose when detection fails.

# One element per line, so sep = "\n" is required. Plain cat(table_md) joins
# the lines with spaces and the table collapses into a single paragraph.
cat(table_md, sep = "\n")

Interpretation Guidelines

2-HT Parameters

dP (Detection of Presence) - 0.0-0.3: Poor detection - 0.3-0.5: Moderate detection - 0.5-0.7: Good detection - 0.7-1.0: Excellent detection

dA (Detection of Absence) - 0.0-0.2: Poor rejection ability - 0.2-0.4: Moderate rejection ability - 0.4+: Good rejection ability

b (Bias) - 0.0-0.1: Low bias (good lineup) - 0.1-0.3: Moderate bias - 0.3+: High bias (problematic lineup)

g (Guessing) - 0.0-0.3: Conservative (prefer rejection) - 0.3-0.7: Moderate - 0.7-1.0: Liberal (prefer selection)

EIG Values

  • 0.0-0.1 bits: Very low diagnosticity
  • 0.1-0.3 bits: Low diagnosticity
  • 0.3-0.5 bits: Moderate diagnosticity
  • 0.5-0.7 bits: Good diagnosticity
  • 0.7+ bits: Excellent diagnosticity

Full ROC AUC

  • 0.50: Chance performance
  • 0.50-0.60: Poor discriminability
  • 0.60-0.70: Fair discriminability
  • 0.70-0.80: Good discriminability
  • 0.80-0.90: Very good discriminability
  • 0.90-1.00: Excellent discriminability

Common Pitfalls

1. Insufficient Sample Size 

# Small sample may lead to unreliable estimates
small_data <- simulate_lineup_data(n_tp = 30, n_ta = 30, d_prime = 1.5, conf_levels = 5)

small_comparison <- compare_models(
  small_data,
  models = c("2ht", "eig"),
  show_warnings = FALSE
)

cat("Warning: Small samples (n=60) may produce unstable parameter estimates\n")
#> Warning: Small samples (n=60) may produce unstable parameter estimates
cat("Recommend: n ≥ 100 per condition for reliable model fitting\n")
#> Recommend: n ≥ 100 per condition for reliable model fitting

2. Model Convergence Issues

If 2-HT model fails to converge: - Check data quality (sufficient variability) - Try different starting parameters - Ensure adequate sample size - Consider data preprocessing

3. Comparing Non-Comparable Measures 

cat("Important: Don't directly compare across models!\n\n")
#> Important: Don't directly compare across models!
cat("✗ Wrong: 'dP = 0.6 is better than EIG = 0.4'\n")
#> ✗ Wrong: 'dP = 0.6 is better than EIG = 0.4'
cat("  → These are different scales and constructs\n\n")
#>   → These are different scales and constructs
cat("✓ Right: 'dP = 0.6 indicates good detection AND\n")
#> ✓ Right: 'dP = 0.6 indicates good detection AND
cat("          EIG = 0.4 indicates moderate diagnosticity'\n")
#>           EIG = 0.4 indicates moderate diagnosticity'
cat("  → Each model provides unique insights\n")
#>   → Each model provides unique insights

Best Practices

1. Fit Multiple Models

Don’t rely on a single model, as each provides unique insights:

# Always fit at least 2-3 models
comprehensive <- compare_models(
  lineup_data,
  models = c("2ht", "eig", "fullroc")
)

cat("Fitting multiple models provides:\n")
#> Fitting multiple models provides:
cat("  • Process-level understanding (2-HT)\n")
#>   • Process-level understanding (2-HT)
cat("  • Overall diagnosticity (EIG)\n")
#>   • Overall diagnosticity (EIG)
cat("  • Threshold-free performance (Full ROC)\n")
#>   • Threshold-free performance (Full ROC)

2. Report All Model Results

When publishing, consider reporting results from all fitted models:

cat("In your paper, report:\n")
#> In your paper, report:
cat("  • 2-HT: Parameters with SE, AIC/BIC, convergence\n")
#>   • 2-HT: Parameters with SE, AIC/BIC, convergence
cat("  • EIG: Value in bits, efficiency percentage\n")
#>   • EIG: Value in bits, efficiency percentage
cat("  • Full ROC: AUC, number of operating points\n")
#>   • Full ROC: AUC, number of operating points
cat("  • Interpretation of each model's insights\n")
#>   • Interpretation of each model's insights

3. Check Model Assumptions 

summary(comparison$fitted_models$`2ht`)
#>

A chi-square p-value below 0.05 indicates that the model does not reproduce the observed response frequencies well. With large samples the test will detect small departures, so read it alongside the size of the discrepancies rather than as a pass/fail.

Technical Details

What each model estimates, and on what scale

The three models are not three estimates of one quantity, and cannot be ranked against each other directly.

Model Estimand Scale Inference available
2-HT Latent probabilities of detection, bias and guessing Four probabilities in [0, 1] Standard errors from the observed information matrix; goodness-of-fit chi-square
EIG Expected reduction in uncertainty about guilt Bits, 0 to the prior entropy None in this package
Full ROC Investigator discriminability AUC in [0.5, 1] None in this package; see the note on ordering bias below

2-HT estimation

The model is a multinomial processing tree. Response probabilities are as given in the introduction, and the parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood over the six observed cell counts (three responses by two lineup types), so the model has four parameters for five free cells and one residual degree of freedom. Standard errors come from the numerically differentiated Hessian at the optimum, and the goodness-of-fit statistic is the usual multinomial chi-square.

Identifiability. The detect-absence parameter dA is identified almost entirely by rejections. If very few witnesses reject, the likelihood is close to flat in dA and the optimiser fails. fit_winter_2ht() checks for this and reports it as such, rather than failing with a message about non-finite differences.

EIG

Expected information gain is computed over the observed response categories with the prior supplied by prior_guilt. Because it is an expectation over a set of categories estimated from the data, it inherits the binning issue discussed in vignette("calibration_decision_analysis"), and it has no standard error here.

Full ROC

Computed as described in vignette("fullroc_analysis"). The default ordering by sample diagnosticity ratio is optimistically biased, because the ordering is estimated from the same data used to compute the area; on data with no signal at all it returns AUC near 0.65 at 100 lineups per arm. compare_models() uses the default ordering, so treat the AUC it reports as an upper bound rather than an estimate, and refit with order = "apriori" for anything inferential.

Assumptions common to all three

  1. Each witness contributes one response, so the response categories partition the sample.
  2. Target-present and target-absent lineups are independent samples.
  3. All lineup members other than the suspect are functioning foils. Where a lineup contains members nobody ever chooses, the effective lineup size is smaller than the nominal lineup_size passed here, and all three models will be misspecified in the same direction.

Summary

Key Functions: - compare_models(): Fit multiple models - print.model_comparison(): View comparison table - summary.model_comparison(): Detailed results - plot.model_comparison(): Visualizations - format_comparison_table(): Publication tables

When to Use Each Model: - 2-HT: Understanding cognitive processes - EIG: Overall diagnosticity assessment - Full ROC: Threshold-free discriminability

Best Practices: - Fit multiple models for comprehensive analysis - Report all model results - Check model fit and convergence - Use adequate sample sizes (n ≥ 100 per condition) - Interpret each model’s unique insights

References

Winter, K., Menne, N. M., Bell, R., & Buchner, A. (2022). Experimental validation of a multinomial processing tree model for analyzing eyewitness identification decisions. Scientific Reports, 12, 15571.

Starns, J. J., Cohen, A. L., & Rotello, C. M. (2023). A complete method for assessing the effectiveness of eyewitness identification procedures: Expected information gain. Psychological Review, 130(3), 677–719. https://doi.org/10.1037/rev0000332

Smith, A. M., Yang, Y., & Wells, G. L. (2020). Distinguishing between investigator discriminability and eyewitness discriminability: A method for creating full receiver operating characteristic curves of lineup identification performance. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 15(3), 589-607.
